metaDescription: Six tent heaters under $150, from an approved radiant propane unit to rated infrared and light ceramic heaters, with ventilation and CO advice for camping.
expertTake: The Mr. Heater Portable Buddy remains the best fuel heater because of its enclosed-use approval and two heat steps. The Dr. Infrared IP55 heater is the best electric pick for a powered camp that sees weather. Never run any fuel heater unventilated or while you sleep. Spend on approval and ventilation habits first, and the choice of model becomes secondary. Keep the receipt for the first trip, and if the heater behaves oddly, return it rather than trusting it with a night in a tent.
introParagraphs: More budget does not make a tent heater safer on its own. What it buys is choice: approved radiant propane designs, weather-rated electric infrared and light ceramic units that suit a car-camping trip.
The same rules apply at every price: ventilate, carry a detector and match output to the tent. The $150 cap reflects listing prices on the date this guide was updated, and prices move.

products.name: Mr. Heater 9,000 BTU Portable Buddy radiant propane heater

specList.label: Approval
specList.value: Designed and approved for indoor and outdoor use

specList.label: Safety
specList.value: Oxygen sensor and tip-over shutoff (maker design)

products.description:
The Portable Buddy gives either 4,000 or 9,000 BTU per hour of radiant heat and is listed as designed and approved for indoor and outdoor use, heating about 225 square feet. Two steps matter in a tent: the low step suits sleeping quarters, and the high step handles a cold start or a big shelter. Mr. Heater builds it with an oxygen depletion sensor and a tip-over shutoff.

Radiant heat warms the people and objects in front of it, so a tent warms unevenly, and the best placement is a few feet from where you sit. Compared with the MOZODAWN, it has a lower maximum output but far better documentation. Compared with the CAMPLUX it adds the indoor approval.

Open two vents, keep a battery CO alarm at head height, keep fabric at the manual's distance and shut the heater off before sleep. Check hose and cylinder connections with soapy water. Think about your sleeping plan before you light it: warm the tent, shut it off, open the vents and rely on a rated bag. Replace the cylinder in the open air, away from flames, and keep a spare.
pros: Approved for indoor and outdoor use
cons: Burns fuel, so ventilation is required
9,000 BTU is too much for small tents

products.name: Dr. Infrared portable heater, IP55, 900/1200/1500W, remote
products.description:
The Dr. Infrared is a plug-in infrared heater with an IP55 rating, three power steps and a remote. IP55 means the housing resists dust and water jets, which is useful at a campsite where dew and rain are common. It makes no combustion gases.

Infrared warms people and objects directly, so it works in drafty or open shelters better than a fan heater. At 1500 watts it makes about 5,100 BTU per hour and draws 12.5 amps, so it needs a real campsite outlet and a short heavy cord. Compared with the Portable Buddy it cannot work off grid, but it removes the CO risk.

Place it on a flat board aimed at the seating, keep fabric three feet away and unplug it when you leave. Use a campsite outlet protected by a ground-fault breaker, and keep the cord out of puddles. Aim the glow at the seating area and keep boots, bags and gear a metre away. The remote is handy when you are already in your sleeping bag.
products.bestFor: Powered camps with a weather-exposed shelter.
pros: Three power steps and a remote

products.name: MOZODAWN 2-in-1 propane heater and stove, 13,000 BTU
products.description:
The MOZODAWN is a heater and stove in one with a 13,000 BTU maximum and 360 degree radiant heat. A stainless threaded interface connects to the cylinder, and it has a carry handle. It is the strongest fuel heater in this guide.

Thirteen thousand BTU is more than a tent needs, and a stove function invites you to cook where you sleep. It suits a large vented shelter or an outdoor gathering. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it has more output but less documented safety approval.

Use it outside, with a CO alarm, and one function at a time. Keep it outside or in an airy shelter, and use the stove function in an open space only. Hose and connector wear are the main ownership issues, so check them each season and replace any suspect part. In ownership terms, the stove side is the part to be careful with: a dual-function appliance is easy to leave in the wrong mode. Close the stove valve when you use it as a heater, and the reverse.
products.bestFor: Large open shelters and outdoor gatherings.

products.name: Trustech 1500W PTC greenhouse heater, 2.5 lb, 90 degree tilt
products.description:
The Trustech is a 1500 watt PTC ceramic heater at only 2.5 pounds with three modes, a 90 degree tilt and overheat protection. It is marketed for greenhouses and garages. It makes no fumes.

At 2.5 pounds it travels easily, but light plastic is less rugged than a milkhouse. Compared with the Dr. Infrared it lacks the weather rating.

Use it on powered sites, dry. It makes sense for people who already pack a 12 volt or power station setup and camp where there is a hookup. Keep it on a flat board, aimed along the floor, and clear of loose fabric. Because both light electric units share the same element and layout, look at the cord length and plug quality when they arrive.

products.name: Air Choice 1500W PTC greenhouse heater, 3.1 lb, carry handle
products.description:
The Air Choice is a close sibling of the Trustech: 1500 watts PTC ceramic, 3.1 pounds, three modes and a carry handle.

It makes no fumes and needs power.

Choose on price. If one of the two light electric heaters is cheaper, buy it, because the differences are small. Both rely on plastic bodies, so protect them from crushing in the gear bin. Plan on a hard flat surface, because a light body on a soft groundsheet can wobble when you brush it. Keep the tilt angle low so warm air heads toward your legs, and avoid blowing it straight at a nylon wall. Dust the grille after dusty trips, and check that the fan spins freely before each use.

products.name: CAMPLUX 8,500 BTU portable propane heater, tripod base
products.description:
The CAMPLUX is an 8,500 BTU propane heater with two speeds, a tilt switch and a detachable tripod base. It weighs 4.2 pounds.

It suits vestibules and open camps.

Ventilate and carry an alarm. The tripod base is a real advantage on uneven ground, and the tilt switch adds a safety net. Keep it for open camps, and let a more documented heater live in the tent. Compared with the Portable Buddy, it has a smaller approval footprint on paper, so treat it as an outdoor or vestibule heater. Take the tripod off for flat ground and use it on uneven ground, and always shield the burner from wind. Carry a spare cylinder and a long lighter, and shut the valve fully before packing.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Portable Buddy is listed as approved for indoor and outdoor use, while the 13,000 BTU MOZODAWN gives more heat with less documentation. In a tent, approval matters more than raw output. A rule of thumb for fuel heaters is to use the smallest output that keeps you comfortable and the largest ventilation you can tolerate. For a family tent of about 100 square feet, think in terms of a few thousand BTU for comfort, and expect higher numbers on the box to be reserve capacity.

The Dr. Infrared is IP55, which resists dust and water jets. The Trustech and Air Choice list no rating, so keep them dry. Check the age of any CO alarm, which usually expires after several years. Open-air cooking and heating in the same shelter doubles the CO sources, so keep the stove outside.

The Trustech is 2.5 lb and the Air Choice 3.1 lb, compared with 4.2 lb for the CAMPLUX. Light helps when you carry gear, but lighter often means less rugged. If you rent a campsite with power, ask what the amp rating is before bringing a heater. If the tent is a modern double-wall design, vents are usually built in, and you should use them all while a fuel heater runs.

Every fuel heater needs two vents and a battery alarm. Electric units remove the risk. A metal heat shield behind the heater protects tent fabric from radiated heat. A cheap plug-in timer rated for the heater's load turns an electric heater off for you, which is a good habit before sleep.

A 1500W heater draws 12.5 amps. Use a short, heavy cord on a dedicated circuit. Do not leave a heater running while you are away from camp. Where weather is changeable, an IP-rated electric heater keeps working when dew and drizzle arrive.

A small tent needs about 3,000 to 4,000 BTU. The MOZODAWN's 13,000 BTU is too much unless the shelter is large. Keep children away from the heater with a physical barrier. Finally, set a rule that nobody sleeps with a fuel heater on, and tell everyone in the group before bed. Replace any heater that has been dropped hard, since internal shutoffs can be damaged without visible signs.

specDecoder.meaning: A maker statement that the heater meets standards for ventilated enclosed spaces. It is the single most important label for a tent. Look for the wording in the manual, not only the listing.
Protection against dust and water jets. It describes the housing, not the heater's life. A higher number means better protection against water.
Heat per hour. It is the total heat per hour. Choose by tent volume.
Radiant heat that warms objects. It warms objects, not air. It heats by glow rather than by blowing air.
An element that limits its own temperature. It limits the element's own temperature. It adds a measure of safety for the element.

cards.label: Fuel
cards.text: The Portable Buddy and MOZODAWN work off grid but need ventilation and a CO alarm.

cards.label: Electric
cards.text: The Dr. Infrared, Trustech and Air Choice make no fumes but need power.

howToChoose.note: Choose electric when there is power. If you camp in rain often, weather rating deserves more weight. For most campers the cheapest safe setup is a campsite hookup and a simple electric heater.
Matching output to tent volume prevents overheating and wasted fuel. Use the high step briefly, then the low step.
A good bag and pad beat any heater. A bag rated below the night temperature solves most cold problems.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You camp in winter and want approval and weather ratings.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You camp in mild weather with power.

howToChoose.note: Spending more buys documented approvals and weather ratings, which are the features that count in a small fabric room.

maintenance.why: Gas leaks are the biggest risk. Skipping this is how a small leak goes unnoticed on a trip. Do it with soapy water and no ignition source nearby.
A dead alarm protects nobody. A dead alarm protects nobody. Do it before every trip, not once a season.
Debris cuts output. Dust and debris lower efficiency. A soft brush is enough, and avoid compressed air near sensors.
A hot plug signals a poor connection. A warm plug is fine; a hot one is not. Pay attention to the plug blades and the strain relief.
Moisture damages igniters. Dry storage prevents rust. A desiccant packet in the box helps.

faq.q: Is the Portable Buddy tent safe?
faq.a: It is approved for ventilated indoor use, but you still need two vents and a CO alarm. Fuel heaters are best treated as a pre-bed warm-up, then switched off.
For a tent, yes. A 1500W electric heater makes the same heat in a tent as in a bedroom, so use the lowest step that keeps you comfortable.
The Dr. Infrared for weather. IP ratings describe the housing, so keep plugs and connections dry as well.
About 12.5 amps at 1500W. If you are not sure a heater suits your tent, check the manual and the tent maker's guidance.

faq.q: Can I sleep with it on?
faq.a: No. A second CO alarm in a group camp is cheap and sensible.

Shield open burners. Whatever heater you choose, a rated sleeping bag and pad should provide your overnight warmth. Many campers find an insulated pad the single best upgrade for cold nights, ahead of any heater. Powered campsites often cap the amps, so ask before arriving.
